When the hour of six o'clock arrived, I had been dealing with certain phases of the contract made with the Grand Trunk Pacific, the specifications, the precautions taken by the government in every detail for the protection of the people of Canada, including a joint supervision by the company and by the -commissioners of the Transcontinental railway on behalf of the government. The hon. member for South Sim-coe (Mr. Lennox), in his remarks, left the inference that there might be collusion between the Grand Trunk Pacific Company and the commission to allow the cost to be very high, for the benefit of somebody not named. Well, Sir, if my hon. friend were in my position for two or three weeks, I think he would
tell the country that there was absolutely no foundation, near or remote, for any such suggestion or insinuation. My experience with the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, and with all railway companies, is that they are quite prepared to take all they can get, and it is no easy task, I assure my hon. friend, to deal with any railway company on behalf of the people of Canada, and give as little as possible to the railway, and guard at eve-jy point possible the interests of the public. Railway companies engage the best men that they can get, and unlike parliaments, they are not bound by any salary limit, they pay as high a salary as is necessary to get the best men, either at home or abroad, legal or business men. It is with these men that the members of the government and their officials have to do business, it is these men we have to meet day after day, and do what we think is right in the interests of the people and not yield one iota that we think is not fair. Now, I want again to impress the House that there is not the remotest foundation for the insinuation; no such idea ever percolated through the mind of any member of the government or any person, that the Grand Trunk Pacific Company and the government are in collusion, or that the Grand Trunk Pacific Company is willing to allow a dollar to be added to the cost of the construction of this road.
Reference was also made to the fact, and it was perhaps the most lengthy part of my hon. friend's remarks, that when contracts were let, the final working out of these contracts did not always substantiate the contention that they had been awarded to the lowest tenderer. To those who have not had some business experience along those lines, that will appear somewhat strong. However, the method adopted by large companies, the method adopted by the best engineers in the world, I think, now, is to let contracts on what is known as schedule rates. They only approximate the -cost, but they put a certain price on every kind of material, so much for earth, so much for loose rock, and so much for solid rock; and although the approximation may seem to a layman very far re>-moved from the reality, the fact remains that the country or the company only pays for the material taken out, and that at the prices named for that material. I discussed the question a good deal with some of my engineers, and other engineers, and they are strongly of the opinion that the fair way to let these contracts, not only on this kind of work, but in all great works, is by .schedule rate; for although they may differ from the approximate cost first worked out, as the quantities may vary somewhat, they do not differ much from the rate named in the contract. These contracts were let in the ordinary way, with the approval of the chief engineer who. with his staff, had the

approximate quantities moneyed out, and they were let to the lowest tenderer in every case.
Now, I come to a point in the discussion which my hon. friend touched upon, and I do not want to be misunderstood at all. We came to a point where the Grand Trunk Pacific itself became a contractor. I discussed this question with Mr. Morse, then general manager, not before they became contractors, because, if I remember correctly, that was before I became a member of the government. But, in discussing the question of the work with him one day, I called his attention to the fact that they had become contractors for the construction of this line. His reason to me was that they had become contractors so that in every case they would tender on work and be prepared to take it at what they thought was a fair value. Any contractor who would accept work at a less rate than the Grand Trunk Pacific offered to do it for would afford fair evidence to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company that they were, getting the work done at a proper value. That was his reason as placed very strongly before me, and I give it to the House and the country. The fact remains that the Grand Trunk Pacific had become contractors. Now, I want to appeal to business men as to the situation as it then struck me and as it still strikes me. Here we found a company that not only was to be the lessee of the line when constructed and to pay the interest on it, but it Was also to be a contracting company, assisting in the building of a line and in addition it was to be the inspector not only of its own work but the inspector of the work of competing contractors. Under these circumstances, a new condition arose altogether. If the Grand Trunk Pacific had not become contractors then I believe there would have been no occasion for the next step that was taken, and was rightly taken as a business step in fairness to all parties. These new conditions having arisen, one can readily understand that the contractors said: We are not only in competition with the Grand Trunk Pacific but we are subjected to the inspection of our competitors as well as that of the government. In order to make it fairer, I and the commissioners too said to the Grand Trunk Pacific: There ought to be some basis arrived at by which you will make the complaints so that no unfairness or injustice may be done to any person. You ought to make your complaints as to classification promptly, you ought to file them so that they can be investigated at once, if necessary, and other contractors besides yourself can settle with their subcontractors without being hindered. If that position were not taken I again appeal to business men if the Grand Trunk Mr. GRAHAM.
Pacific would not have been in the position of being able to hold up every bit of work on the eastern part of the Transcontinental railway. By refusing or neglecting to inspect or pass upon work they could have made it impossible for any other contractor to complete any work that he had undertaken. That would not have been in the interest of the work, that would not have been in the interest of the country and it certainly would have been a great injustice to the men in the Dominion of Canada who invest their money in contracting. So, we did have a conference- nothing secret about the conference. My hon. friend seemed to rather ridicule the idea. It was a straight business proposition, above board and nothing whatever secret about it. We did have a conference, and at that conference, if I remember correctly, were Mr. Hays, possibly his engineer, Mr. Parent, I think Mr. Biggar, their solicitor, and one or two members of the government, including myself. After a good deal of discussion the situation as it existed was pointed out, and I take the full responsibility for pointing it out. I said: We ought to come to some arrangement by which these complaints as to classification, or as to anything else, shall be made promptly and so that in no case can a contractor be held up by the Grand Trunk Pacific as being an interested party, as contractors as well as inspectors. After the discussion on January 10, 1908, this memorandum was drawn up:
Monthly estimates for contractors shall be submitted promptly from time to time by the chief engineer of the commissioners to the company's assistant chief engineer at Montreal for approval. If he has any objection to such estimates he shall promptly file the same with the chief engineer of the commissioners, and any objections from time to time filed shall thereupon be considered, and, if possible, determined by the said engineers, and in case of their failure to agree, may then or at any time before or at the time of the final payment, at the option of either party, be considered and determined by arbitration as provided in the agreement of the 29th July, 1903, but in no case shall the payment of monthly estimates be delayed except with the consent of the commissioners.
In case the chief engineer of the commissioners and the assistant chief engineer of the company disagree as to the final payment, the same shall he withheld until the matter is determined by arbitration, as provided in the said agreement of 29th July, 1903.
This memorandum was initialled by Mr. C. M. Hays, Mr. Lumsden and the Hon. Mr. Parent. After this memorandum was agreed to, the progress estimates were sent to the Grand Trunk Pacific at Montreal, and objections were subsequently filed by Mr. Woods on behalf of the company as to classifications in districts ' B ' and ' F and ' over-break ' in the latter district.

If such had been the case no such memorandum would have been drawn up, because we would have done just what the Grand Trunk Pacific wanted, or they would have done just what we wanted. We now come to a point in the discussion of this question where difficulties seemed to arise. It had been a rather strenuous undertaking to get this board of arbitrators formed and if my hon. friend who spoke so strongly this afternoon had been a party to getting it formed he never would have made the insinuation he did this afternoon that there was any chance of collusion by the government with the Grand Trunk Pacific in reference to this board.
I may mention here a certain memorandum of agreement to which my hon. friend referred this afternoon as having been sent by the Grand Trunk Pacific to the commissioners for their signatures. It was quite a lengthy document and purported to be an agreement to be signed by the minister or the commission, I forget which, and already signed by the Grand Trunk officials, pointing out how this work of arbitration was to be carried on. The chairman of the commission declined to sign that memorandum of agreement prepared by the Grand Trunk officials, and said that the work would be carried on under the terms of the statute and the agreement. That was not an agreement, it was a piece of paper on which certain things w'ere written by the Grand Trunk Pacific and signed by them and which they asked to have made an agreement by having attached to it the signature of the government or the Transcontinental Commission, which was never done.
_ The board went west and started to work, just after Mr. Schreiber's appointment. In a short time they returned from the west, certain objections having been made to their work. The board started to work and immediately there were protests from the engineers in charge. I want to ask hon. gentlemen one question. I do not know whether the board of arbitration were carrying out their work properly or not, I am not here to judge, but I ask hon. gentlemen to say, if they were in the position of these engineers-and my remark is fully substantiated by my hon. friend's words this afternoon-whose reputation as engineers, whose characters for honesty, and ability were at stake in this work being performed, if these gentlemen had been in the position of these engineers and thought their work was not

~
being fairly arbitrated upon would they not have done just what the engineers did? I am free to say that I would have done the same thing. I come now to the objections raised by the engineers. I have referred to their objections before and do not propose to go into them at any length because they are all in the correspondence brought down to the House; but several of the divisional engineers did make certain complaints and placed them before the commissioners. They did so, I think, on the same day that Mr. Lumsden resigned, but before his resignation was submitted to the board, if I remember correctly. The summing up of their objections is to be found in these paragraphs:
(a)	That they were based in whole or in part on the said draft agreement of May 14th, 1909, which bad been rejected, and which had no existence in fact;
(b)	That the examination of the work was
of a liascy, insufficient and superficial character ;	'
(c)	That the engineers on the line who classified the work were not afforded a sufficient hearing and an opportunity of presenting evidence;
(d)	That the contractors were not afforded an opportunity of showing cause: and further to say that the commissioners insist, in the
public interest, that the proceedings of the arbitration tribunal shall be exhaustive, final and conclusive; shall cover all the objections filed on behalf of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and that the report of the arbitrators, when made, shall be supported by substantial evidence, including details of quantities, &c., which will safeguard the position of the commissioners in any litigation which may arise with the contractors as a result of any action which may follow the report of the board of arbitration.
Sir, whatever differences there may be among us, if the board of arbitration finally bring in a report according to clause (d) of these objections, that wifi cover everything that could be covered by any board of arbitration or by any tribunal. The question was put to me before recess how it could be possible that the commissioners could in any way represent the people and I was asked to give an illustration. It is possible that a case might arise, if the engineers in charge were not given full opportunity to make their side of the case clear and give reasons for their classifications, if the fullest evidence were not taken and placed on record a case might arise in which the contractor could collect from the government and the government could not get the interest from the Grand T'-unL-Pacific. The Grand Trunk Pacific and tn~ government have a contract which provid'd for an adjustment of any differences between them by a board of arbitration and under which the government, would collect interest on the amounts established by the board as the cost of construction. But if the evidence were not sufficiently complete to substantiate the findings of the board, a condition might easily arise under which the contractor could collect a greater amount from the government than the gov eminent could compel the Grand Trunk Pacific to pay interest on; and that is where the commissioners would stand for the interests of the people in making the Grand Trunk Pacific pay interest on the amount .the government might be compelled to pay under the contract. My hon. friend from North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) saw the point at a glance the other day because he put a question on the order paper to this effect: Does the government intend to hold the contractors responsible for any reduction in classification and if so are the contractors to be represented on the board of arbitration? The hon. member for North Ontario with his legal acumen, saw exactly the situation. He saw that it might be possible for the contractors to collect from the government an amount greater than the amount on which the government could collect interest from the Grand Trunk Pacific, so that in order to protect the people it is absolutely necessary that every finding of the board of arbitration shall be sub-
stantiated by evidence that could be taken in the Exchequer Court in support of the government's contentions.
Is the defence of the engineers published in their evidence?
There are two or three letters in sessional paper 42a.

No, what they complained of is that they were not allowed to give any evidence before the board, and they protested that they should be allowed to give evidence to show why they made their classifications.
Have they not done that at any time since?

Not that I am aware of. I do not know just all the details, but some adjustment work has been done. The chief engineers have come to an agreement concerning some of their differences. In one division in one contract, they have practically settled all the differences between them-that is after the new board was constituted and Mr. Grant became chief engineer.
As regards Mr. Lumsden's resignation, I would not criticise a man of his intelligence, ability and integrity. Mr. Lums-den has been known in this country a great number of years, and I have the utmost respect for him, but I think his friends will not find it amiss if I make this comment. Had I been chief engineer, and had my instructions not been carried out, I would never have resigned but would have seen that the other men, who did not carry out my instructions, were forced to resign. After all, whatever deviations from duty occurred, if any there were, they all come back to this, that the chief engineer was responsible, not only for the instructions he gave, but also for the carrying out of his instructions. Had I been chief engineer, no combination of circumstances would have driven me from my post, but I would have stayed and insisted on the dismissal of any engineer who disobeyed my instructions. About the time of the resignation, I was absent from the country, and during my absence another chief engineer was appointed; but on my return from the old country, I wrote this letter, which it may not be necessary to quote, but which I think it is just as well to put on record.

Dear Mr. Parent,-As I was leaving for Europe some time ago the resignation of the Mr. GRAHAM.
chief engineer of the commission, Mr. Lums-den, was received, and I left it with my colleagues for consideration. I find on my return that in his letter of resignation Mr. Lumsden intimated that he had lost confidence in certain of his staff.

AVhat you desire and what we all desire is justice to all parties and the fullest protection of the public interest. Any employee who has forgotten this, or has failed to act on this principle cannot be retained for a moment.

Ottawa, September 2, 1909.
The Honourable

Graham, P.C.,
Minister of Railways and Canals.
Dear Mr. Graham,-The views expressed in your letter of the 31st ultimo coincide exactly with our own, and I need hardly say that we are prepared at all times to act along these lines in the matter of our staff and any other within our control which might affect public interest.
Should any reasonable proof be brought that employees in our service had been guilty of serious negligence or wrong-doing, you can rest assured that Commissioners would deal prompt justice, as we have done already in several cases.
It is not a vain word to say that our engineers in the field can bear comparison with those on any other railroad. Most of them have been connected with the National Transcontinental railway since its earliest stage, when comprehensive surveys had to be carried on from one end of the year to the other, through a rough and distant region, amid great hardships. Was it not because the matter was under adjudication of the arbitrator, and so Mr. Woods took the position that there was no occasion for this inspection?

I do not know. I merely state that Mr. Woods did not accompany Mr. Grant and that Mr. Grant went over the line alone. But the terms of the agreement are that, in case of a dispute arising, if possible, a settlement shall be arranged by the chief engineers, and only such things are referred to arbitration "as the chief engineers fail to agree upon. If the chief engineers agree, then, even if the third arbitrator were on the ground, there is no need for him to give advice in the matter. But, if the chief engineers come to a section where they cannot agree, the third arbitrator steps in and makes a decision for them. Now, there was a reduction, I think, of $370,000 altogether on the McArthur contract, and it is only fair to say that all this was not made by Mr. Grant, There was an amount made before Mr. Grant became chief engineer of this division, and it reduced the amount of the reduction made to $202,402. I think it is not unfair to say that it may be, when the final adjudication comes, that Mr. Grant made too great a reduction, possibly; or it might transpire he had not made reduction enough. But this is the amount, in order that the commission might be on the safe side.
That action is final, is it not?
Let me call the minister's attention to a letter written by Mr. Woods to Mr. Grant, dated July 22,' 1909, in which he says:	'

' ifl arbitrators have been over the line, and while their report has not been made, or at least has not been seen by the writer, I do not consider it advisable that I should visit, the work and personally agree with you on the points which may have been caken under consideration by the board of arbitrators, and might, to a certain extent, impair such report when made.

Then I will retract what I said that Mr. Wood was at Prince Rupert, he was in _ Montreal and did not go. However, I think I am quite clear that that position was shortly afterwards abandoned by the company. Now I want to read the_ letter signed by Mr. Gordon Grant which explains these reductions:
Ottawa, September 20, 1909. The Commissioners of the Transcontinental Railway, Ottawa, Out.
With reference to my letter of the 14th instant re my_ recent inspection of district ' F/ and in which I stated that I was deducting $370,000 from the progress estimates now due Mr. McArthur. Since writing that letter I have revised my figures, and the amount to be deducted now is $359,488.96, and my construction accountant has since informed me that Mr. Lumsden had previously deducted $140,086.80 from McArthur's March estimate, .and $17,000 from the April estimate, but for what reason I do not know, though I presume it was for overbreak, but he has left no record or memorandum showing from what residency, sub-contractor or cutting he %vished the above amount deducted.
Consequently, as I am satisfied that, for the present purposes, and until the arbitration has taken place, the above mentioned amount is sufficient to hold back. I have signed McArthur's estimates to date, after deducting the $359,488.96, less the amount previously deducted by Air. Lumsden, viz., $157,086.80, which will amount to a deduccion on my part of $202,402.16.
I may say here that there is another deduction made on the Grand Trunk Pacific of $15,000. Now Mr. Grant and Mr. Schreiber went to Winnipeg to meet Mr. Kelliher, on September 30, 1909. I may explain, as my hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) intimates in his contention, that the Grand Trunk Pacific contended that there was no need to appoint a new: board of arbitrators, that the resignation of Mr. Lumsden 'did not necessitate a new appointment of a board of arbitrators, but that the appointment of Mr. Grant as chief engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific merely filled the vacancy, and consequently any work done by the board of arbitrators stood as the work of the board, and the mere; change of the personnel did not make any change in the situation. Well, as against that, as against the contention of Mr. Chamberlain, who also took that ground, and there is no doubt Mr. Woods was acting under the instruction of Mr. JANUARY 25, 1910
Chamberlain in not going to , the west, I wish to put on record the opinion of Mr. Newcombe, the deputy minister:
Ottawa, September 28, 1909. The Deputy Minister of Justice, Canada,
I am of opinion, upon perusal of the annexed correspondence and of sections 7 and 4 of the agreement, that, Mr. Lumsden having resigned, it is necessary, or at least advisable, for Mr. Grant, his successor and Mr. Kelliher to join in a new appointment of Mr. Schreiber as third arbitrator.
E. L. NEWCOMBE, Deputy Minister.
Consequently the position of the commissioners, the position of the government, and the position of Mr. Grant, was upheld by the deputy minister of justice, and on his advice they were acting in saying that it was wise, if not absolutely necessary, that Mr. Schreiber be reappointed chairman by the new board as constituted including Mr. Grant, the new chief engineer. They went to the west to meet Mr. Kelliher to join in a new work of arbitration, or to proceed with the work. Now it will be said, and fairly said, that there was a great deal of dispute as to the methods to be adopted by this new board of arbitrators when they got to the west. The board of commissioners contended, and I think wisely, acting on the advice of the deputy minster of justice, first, that Mr. Schreiber had to be appointed anew, or, as the lawyers would say, de novo. They contended also that the work of arbitrations so far done ought to be recommended, or that the work ought to be started and done all over again under conditions that would meet the objection, namely, that all the evidence ought to be placed on record, and every fact stated, so that the finding of the arbitrators would be a finding upheld by the Exchequer Court in case of a suit between the contractors and the Transcontinental Railway Commission.
Did the Minister of Justice agree to that?
The Minister of Justice was in London at the time, and the deputy acting for him gave his opinion.
Not in that direction.

It was merely as to the methods to, be adopted, as to the mode of procedure which was to be taken on the arbitration. Mr. Kelliher refused altogether at first to sign the appointment of Mr. Schreiber anew. But after discussion, these disagreements as to the scope of the arbitration, as to whether it should be confined to the agreement made by the Grand Trunk
Pacific with the commission, the other agreement made by the Grand Trunk Pacific and the commission as to the filing of complaints promptly, as to the interpretation of classification agreed upon between them, they did not agree, and Mr. Kelliher, I understand, refused to sign the appointment of Mr. Schreiber. No one can claim that the refusal was the fault of the commission, because that appointment was in the identical language of the appointment signed before by Mr. Kelliher. But it was upon that point, and I am not going to argue as to the right of the Grand Trunk Pacific to take it. They contended it was not necessary to reappoint him, and refused to sign his reappointment. They returned again without doing anything; and as my hon. friend said this afternoon, it seemed as if it was impossible to have anything done. But I submit in all fairness that it was not the fault of the government or of the commission that these arbitrators did not proceed, it was the fault of neither that it did not proceed months before it did, because, in all Mr. Lumsden's correspondence he complained that he could not get an arbitrator appointed. But in so many circumstances and so many details, it is not a matter of great surprise that strong opinions might be formed. But after the return of these commissioners from the west, it seemed there was only one way to proceed to get a third arbitrator appointed. Now the question was raised: Should Mr. Schreiber be reappointed to the position? I took the position strongly, and my colleagues upheld me, that Mr. Schreiber was an able and intelligent man, of uprightness and integrity, and the government having appointed Mr. Schreiber, they were satisfied to have him reapp_ointed anew as the third arbitrator in these proceedings.
But, Sir, as I have pointed out nothing was done and that without any fault either of the government, or of the commission, or of the new chief engineer of the commission. When the arbitrators returned from the west I think one or two conferences were held between the Grand Trunk Pacific railway and the commission to see if they could not arrive at some conclusion to proceed with this arbitration. It seemed impossible to arrive at such a conclusion, and the commission, acting under the statute, applied to the Chief Justice on November 11, 1909, to appoint a third arbitrator. I referred a moment ago to the reasons why it was necessary that the greatest and strictest care be taken in the work of these arbitrators so that their finding might be based on evidence which w^ould be sufficient td protect the government against contractors being able to collect from them an amount greater than the amount they could 0001-" pel the Grand Trunk Pacific to pay interest on under their lease. What is the situation? I have pointed out as rapidly and as clearly as I could the different steps that have been taken along the line in reference to this work. I submit that the government and the commission has done its best to get these difficulties settled, because it was in the interest of all parties before the sub-contractors were settled with and the final acceptance of the work by the Grand Trunk Pacific should be accomplished-I don't mean the taking over of the road for leasing purposes, but the acceptance of it by their engineers as completed work-that such adjustment should take place. The point has been raised somewhere by somebody at some time, that the government might be responsible to the sub-contractors, or rather to the contractors themselves for the payment to the sub-contractors. That is far from being the case. The commission has no contract with any persons but the chief contractors, or the contractors in the first instance, and any arrangement these contractors may have with the subcontractors, or with the secondary sub-contractors is no concern of the commission' so far as the .settlement goes. If the contractors themselves have settled in full .with the sub-contractors and an amount is deducted from the chief contractors, they have to bear the loss and look out for any, reimbursement they can get from the subcontractors. Personally, I am inclined to think, notwithstanding anything that has been said, that the chief contractors have likely looked out all along the line and have probably protected themselves largely from any such thing as the sub-contractors being over-paid. But if they have not, that is their concern not ours. The commission deals only with the chief contractors and not with the sub-contractors. But, Sir, is the country protected? As my hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Haggart) will understand perhaps better than any one in the House-no doubt better than I do, he-f cause he has had such great experience- in all_ these contracts a certain amount of deposit is required when the contracts are let, and in addition to that undeT the terms, of the agreement which I read this afternoon, ten per cent of the amount actually expended is deducted monthly and held, back from the contractors and repaid tq them after two months if it be found that the money can be used properly in a more rapid prosecution of the work. In addition to that, all the plant belonging to these companies forms part of the security for the completion of the work on the ground.
I want to call the attention of the House and the country to the fact that notwithstanding all that has been said, there is a large amount of money in the hands of the government to-day to protect the government against"any over-classification that may be found along the line of the Trans-, continental railway. In this, as in other parts of the contract, the government has been very careful to guard its position. I have tried to get these figures into such form that they will be applicable to the situation and be a conclusive argument on that point, and as such I present them to the House.

I thought I had produced documents which were sufficient evidence that the government had been endeavouring to refer this matter to arbitration for months and months and were not able to get the desired result until they appealed to the Chief Justice for the appointment of the third arbitrator and then the Grand Trunk Pacific agreed to the appointment of a third man who was appointed and the commission has the work m hand.
As I said, the whole thing comes back to the question of over-classification, and parliament, I want to repeat, in its wisdom, Mr. GRAHAM.
without any objection, decided, and wisely, that any cases, whether of classification oi differences of opinion as to work of this kind which should come up, should be referred to three expert engineers, who are better judges than any Committee of this House or even the Exchequer Court, and it is no disrespect to say that concerning the Exchequer Court, because if this had been left to the decision of the Exchequer Court the judge would probably have referred it to the Board of Engineers to decide, and on their report he would have acted. That has been done time and time again, as my hon. friend knows.
As I said, the people want to know about the cost of this railway, and eventually, they shall know all about it, the details, everything will be examined, investigated and sifted by the tribunals appointed for that purpose. As I said to Mr. Parent returning from Europe: If it be found that, any engineer or employee of the Transcontinental railway has been guilty of wrong conduct I will be the first to ask that he be dismissed and dismissed summarily, but I never ask that to be done with a man until he has had a proper opportunity to show whether or not he is deserving of that treatment.	,
As I said, what the people want to know is about the value of this work. I may, I think, without offence, recall to my hon. friend from South Sinicoe the fact that all the horrible details that could be conceived by the most fertile imagination as to the cost or presumed cost of this railway were placed before the people of Canada in 1908. Every exaggeration that could be imagined, as to what would be the ultimate cost was preached from every platform in this province and, I think, in every province of the Dominion. What was the verdict of the people? The verdict of the! people was: We want the road, and we want the party who are friends of the road, to finish it in the interests of the people. Hon. gentlemen opposite, while pretending to be in favour of this road, give it what my countrymen would call the Irishman's affection, they give it a kick first and then expect to be considered its friend. This road has been projected by the Prime Minister of the Dominion of Canada, and his name will be connected with it, and I say, notwithstanding all that has been urged against the project, that when history becomes to be written, the name of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the Grand Trunk Pacific will be upon its pages to the credit of both, and that this road will work a wonderful development in the transportation problem of this Dominion, which is now the great question before the people. It has its difficulties, it has its troubles, no one knows the difficulties surrounding a work of this kind under government man-

ageinent better than I do myself. I do not ask for sympathy from any man living on account of the difficulties, I do the best I. can, I grapple with them, honestly and fairly. If I make mistakes, they are not made wilfully, they are made with honesty of purpose, and I challenge any hon. gentleman to point to a single act of mine in ' connection with this road that will not bear the utmost scrutiny from the public standpoint.
This work has been undertaken by the Liberal party, it is a work for the national benefit, it is something not contemplated by any party before, because hon. gentlemen opposite when constructing one of the same kind spent nearly as much and did not own a foot of railway when it was completed.

I think my hon. friend can answer that himself. This government will own 1,804 miles under lease to the Grand Trunk Pacific for fifty years. I am willing to leave this case to the country. Parliament itself has named the tribunal and provided for its formation. The government and the commission are willing to leave the decision to the tribunal appointed by this parliament. If, after they have concluded their labours, it be found that parliament or the country are not satisfied with their findings, parliament is supreme to do whatever it chooses; but I submit as a business man to business men, I submit to men of legal learning and experience, that it would not be wise, it would not be expedient, it would not be carrying out the terms of our contract with the Grand Trunk Pacific, if we proposed now to go into an investigation of a matter which is-already before a tribunal selected for that purpose by us.	.
Mr, FOSTER. Might I put a question? Will the hon. minister be good enough to explain just what this committee, which is to be appointed under this resolution, is to investigate? We have heard what it is not to investigate. Would the hon. gentleman give us an idea now as to what it is going to investigate? If he would, he will certainly enlighten me and other members.

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: It is rather wearisome, but I shall read again the resolution for the benefit of my hon. friend.

speechtext: I would ask the hon. minister to dispense. What I want from him is an explanation of that resolution. Any man ean read it, but we do not all grasp what it means.

speechtext: My hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Haggart), with his usual precision, puts the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) right. He says the last paragraph explains it. I will read that.
