speechtext:
I do not see that I can use any plainer language:
Therefore, it is resolved, that a special committee of five members of the House, to be named hereafter, be appointed to investigate the said charges and allegations of the said Hugh D. Luinsden against a portion of the said engineering staff of the said railway; that such committee have power to send for persons, papers and records, to examine persons on oath or affirmation, and to report from time to time.
Mr. Lumsden has made certain charges and they are to be investigated.

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: What are the charges?

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: My hon. friend will find them in Mr. Lumsden's letter read by myself and by the Prime Minister.

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: Would my hon. friend tell us what they are in his own language?

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: I would not like to detain the House longer recapitulating what is so plain. I submit that the charges made by Mr. Lumsden should be investigated by a committee, and that the Board of Engineers, as regards the classifications, should be allowed to complete its work, as provided by the agreement embodied in the statute. In my opinion, the people have confidence in the government, they have confidence that the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific is for the benefit of Canada, that it is being constructed as economically as possible, and that their interests are safe in the hands of the Liberal party. The government, on its part, is prosecuting this undertaking to its ultimate conclusion so that the people may have the benefit, outlined by the Prime Minister, when he first introduced the resolution, and that is the solving of the transportation problem from east to west and from west to east. I submit therefore that the amendment to the resolution should not be carried, but that the motion of the Prime Minister should pass.

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I rather congratulate my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) on the question he put a moment ago to the Minister of Railways because he drew from that hon. gentleman, in the last five minutes of his long speech, the only words he addressed to the subject matter of the resolution. For two hours we had the hon. minister addressing us upon every matter connected with the Transcontinental except the subject brought before the House by the Prime Minister. He discussed the contract, the specifications, the amended specifications, the arbitration, the correspondence of the arbitrators-everything which has no rela-

turn whatever to the resolution, and it was only during the last five minutes that he said anything about the resolution itself. With all respect to the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) and without any desire to be in the least degree offensive, I would like to say that, in order to take up as little as possible of the time of the House unnecessarily. I shall not at all refer to the nineteen-twentieths of the speech he has just delivered.
The subject before us is a very simple one. It has nothing whatever to do with the arbitration. If the Grand. Trunk railway had accepted every certificate, if they had agreed to every expenditure, if they made not the least objection to any expenditure by the commissioners, that would have nothing whatever to do with our objection to the narrow scope of the reference proposed by the Prime Minister. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways has told us over and over again that the people of this country want this railway and mean to pay for it. I do not suppose that any one say's the contrary. We want the railway and we intend to pay for it, and no doubt we shall be made to pay for it. But is that any reason why we should be swindled? Is that any reason why the country should be robbed? Is that any reason -why there should be malversation, misconduct, incompetence or criminal negligence? Are we to be silent and make no inquiries when we are told time and again that there has been conduct in the management and construction of this railway amounting to fraud. Are we to be content with a long speech from the Minister of Railways about arbitration and specifications and not one word in reproba-tion-if the charges be true-of what Mr. Lumsden has alleged in his letter of June last. Surely whatever questions or disputes there may be between the Grand Trunk Pacific Company and the commissioners of the government, no one will pretend for a moment that the existence of such disputes can justify or exercise any neglect to investigate the misconduct charged by Mr. Lumsden. My whole object in rising is ito add something to what has been said by the Prime Minister and my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) as to the gravity of this matter. The Prime Minister, in his resolution, says that the charges are grave and demand investigation. We agree with him, but we say that the charges are so serious that they demand investigation beyond the scope indicated in the resolution. That is the whole question. There is no other question between the two sides of this House. We are all agreed' that there should be an investigation; but whether that investigation shall be confined to a few staff officers and a few engineers and to certain portions of certain districts, or

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext:
whether it shall go to the bottom and find out whether such wrong doings as are complained of exist anywhere and who are responsible, is the question at issue. We on this side say that the investigation should not be confined to the question whether a few subordinate engineers have done wrong. The question is, has any wrong been done and who is responsible?
I listened with a good deal of attention to the Minister of Railways and Canals. I hoped he would, somehow or other, get to the question, but I failed to see that he has shown himself able to appreciate the position he occupied as Minister of Railways towards these commissioners. The hon. gentleman set out, at the very beginning, with a glorification of the position- there were contracts entered into between these contractors and the government; we had the commission there with its chief engineer, and the chief engineer had great and important duties to perform. We all know these things, but these are not matters in the question. It comes down to this -that since Mr. Hodgins made his charges there have been like complaints of improper conduct, yet no adequate investigation has been made on the part of the government. The hon. minister complimented my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) on the work he had done in going carefully through these contracts and the moneys that nad been paid on them and on the ability he displayed in 'criticising the acts of those in authority. Sir, we know that if the Minister of Railways had been doing his duty, every figure that the hon. member for South Simcoe worked out today would have 'been in his department month by month since the. time these contracts were entered into. There is not a railway company in the world that, entering into such contracts as these based on surveys and rough estimates-more or less precise-and finding as they would soon have found, that the outlay was more than they had anticipated, but would have checked these payments by the specifications and estimates laid before the contractor in order to learn the explanation of this enormous and unexpected increase. Where do we find the first attempt on the part of the minister, with his great staff of skilful and able officers, to check these estimates month by month as they came in. If that had been done, as it would have been done in any business office, the minister would have known that things were going wrong and would not have had to wait for two or three years and until millions had been squandered before he made an attempt at investigation.
I wish to point out as briefly as I can

a few things which will indicate how negligent the Railway Department has been, how little alive to what is going on, and how little careful to forestall any improper practices. To appreciate the gravity of this question, you have only to go over some of the figures back to the year 1907-8. It was in 1908 that Mr. Hodgins made his charges, almost identical even in wording with the later charges of Mr. Lumsden, and almost identical with the complaints made by Mr. Woods, of the Grand Trunk Pacific. The words are almost copied from each other-they refer to the same specifications-and you find, if you read the letter of Mr. Lumsden of June 25th last, that he declares to be going on at that time just what Mr. Hodgins said was going on in March, 1908.
Now, let us see how much has been expended on the construction of the two sections ' B ' and ' F,' which are the two indicated by Mr. Hodgins, frequently referred to by Mr. Woods and more recently referred to by Mr. Lumsden, In the report of the Transcontinental Commissioners for 1908, page 41, you find that the commission expended for the year ending March 31, 1908, on section 'B,' $8,467,124. Then there is the 'contract reserve,' arid I give this figure now because of the boastful language of the minister when he was speaking of the amount they had in hand. This reserve is shown by the Transcontinental Commission to be only $299,569. This leaves the cash paid out for one year on section ' B,' $8,167,554. In the same year, as stated at nage 46, the amount paid out on district 'F' was $8,155,864. That is, on these two districts, which have been subject to such charges as compelled the Prime Minister to ask for a committee, they spent in one year-the year which was the period of Mr. Hodgins charges-$16,323,419. In the next year up to March 31, 1909, they expended on sections 'B' and 'F,' $17,920,992. For these two years there was spent on districts 'B' and 'F' the enormous sum of $34,244,411. Now, we are within two months of the completion of another year, on March 31. If you add another year at the same rate as these others, you find that in the years 1908, 1909 and 1910. we shall have spent about $51,000,000 on these two sections. That is, in these three years, taking no account of what was spent before 1908, or of what will be spent in the year that is soon to open, they have expended fully as much as the Minister of Finance said would build the whole railway from Moncton to Winnipeg.
I take those figures as showing in a manner that cannot be disputed, in clear and concise way, the enormous amount that is being expended beyond anybody's anticipation. Here we find that, in three years only of the five or six years it is 77
going to take to build that road, we have spent on districts ' B ' and ' F ' where these charges apply, more than we were assured by the Finance Minister would build the whole eastern section of 1,800 miles. Now when you look at that, and when you consider that Mr. Hodgins made the specific charge in 1908, that the Grand Trunk Pacific engineer confirms that charge in letter after letter, and on that on June 25 of last year, Mr. Lumsden, the chief engineer, repeats the charge specifically, and rather than submit to the degradation and shame of assisting in such misconduct as he refers to that he throws up a valuable appointment and	goes out	of the	servicesurely you cannot imagine any stronger reason for	an	inquiry. There cannotbe the slightest dispute on that point, it seems to me. I do not care to go into all these details. What the hon. member for North Simeoe has worked out so elaborately ought to be in the office of the minister; he ought to have had that information	month by	month	since thework began. The engineers in his department could do that, and should have done	it.	They	should	have therecords at hand, and ought to be able to confirm or dispute every word the hon. gentleman recited here.	,
Now where are we on this question? Are we to submit, because we are building a railway, to robbery? because it is robbery, and nothing short of robbery. When we take that letter of Mr. Lumsden where he says his orders have been disobeyed; where he charges specific improper acts, and that these have been going on, and that in consequence he has lost all confidence in the engineers on a certain portion of the railway, can we doubt that it is our duty to insist on a thorough and complete inquiry?
But the Prime Minister says: Oh, we will inquire into the conduct of these few men, these few officials, who axe charged specifically by Mr. Lumsden. He assumes, apparently, that Mr. Lumsden having recently gone over ' B ' and ' F ' and seeing these things, and in his indignation, having resigned, that he forsooth acquits all others on the whole railway. What an absurdity. If a commission were investigating this matter, and they got up to a certain mile post and discovered such things as are here charged, would they stop and say: We assume the mischief didn't go beyond that mile post, or would they say: We will go on and see what has occurred beyond. Surely a business man would. Surely if this was the case of a great corporation, and they had found peculation and robbery, and shameful misconduct among their staff, they would not think of dismissing only two or three caught, as you may say, in the act,

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in all candour I think the House will agree after the statement of hon. members on the other side who addressed the House on this subject to-day that they never expected, never hoped and knew that they had no right to expect or to hope that the resolution which they have proposed would be adopted. The hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) has said that- Mr. Lumsden went up, inspected sections ' B ' and ' F,' got mad with some body and apparently mad with himself, went off in a pet and came home and resigned. Because Mr. Lumsden stated in his letter to the commission that he had lost confidence in some of the engineering staff, whom he had himself appointed, because they disobeyed his instructions, not on the whole line of the

Transcontinental, not on the whole line of the eastern division, not on the whole of sections 'B' and 'F,' but simply on a small portion of these sections, because he was in a pet according to the hon. member for Hamilton, as against some of his own engineers, therefore, hon. gentlemen opposite say that we mu3t appoint a roving commission and investigate this whole Transcontinental railway from one end of it to the other. That is the logic and argument of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. I think we ought to understand what may be called the fair ground for parliamentary investigation. I think it is not stating it improperly to say that if a prima facie case is shown parliament should investigate any wrong-doing or any abuse where such an investigation would result in any advantage or have any purpose. But parliament should not lend itself to purposeless or resultless investigation, or where matters are sub judice, or where an investigation is proposed without ground or warrant and solely for political purposes. I submit that that statement of the duty of parliament is absolutely correct, will be found to be based upon precedent, and is manifestly adaptable to the present occasion. This matter is now sub judice in the hands of the very tribunal to which parliament said it should go five years ago and to which my hon. friends sitting on the other side of the House-and I have read the debate upon this subject and they certainly discussed the Transcontinental Railway Bill at length enough-agreed. The hon. gentlemen who are to-day raising this issue agreed to the passage of this section 7 without any question whatever. That tribunal was created after all the deliberation and all the discussion that took place as to which was the best way to settle technical questions which might arise as to the correctness or incorrectness of engineering views and as to classification. That tribunal has been appointed, it is now dealing with the matter and although the question is sub judice my hon. friends ask this House-I say it not without the most absolute confidence-solely for political purposes to take the matter out of the hands of that tribunal which has been created for that purpose and to engage in a purposeless investigation. That is the situation as it exists to-day. What is the occasion for this debate? Mr. Lumsden, who was the chief engineer of the Transcontinental Railway company, in resigning his position, said that certain engineers, whom he himself had appointed, had disobeyed his instructions and acted in bad faith. My right hon. friend the leader of the House (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) asks this House to investigate that statement and to ascertain whether it is a fact or not. That 77i
is how it has come here. If all this great necessity for an investigation with regard to the operation and construction of the Transcontinental railway existed that these hon. gentlemen have conjured up with solemn faces and deep intonations and which according to their story has existed for the past two years. We have been sitting for nearly two months and these gentlemen have sat inert and have not attempted before to save this country from the terrible catastrophe that they would like us to believe is threatening. This government come with thi3 motion in the proper way, according to the rules of parliament and ask parliament to investigate a statement of the chief engineer to ascertain whether it was bad faith, whether there had been a breach of instructions to which these gentlemen, employing that large amplitude of adjectives which they always bring forward whenever they smell a scandal, propose an amendment. What do they say? They say:
H. I). Lumsden, in tendering his resignation as chief engineer of the N. T. Ry., has made grave charges-
Grave charges, say they.
-touching the expenditure of public moneys' in the construction of the said railway, which charges ought, in the public interest, to be thoroughly investigated.
Is there anything in that language or in that paragraph which involves a single thing in any degree greater or wider than the words stated in the government resolution? Not a single thing. We have a lot of superlatives there put in for effect in order that our Conservative friends may furnish material to their newspapers throughout the country, all those adjectives are supplied for that purpose, but when you come down to analyse it, when you come to the final analysis as the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) says, you will find that this section of the resolution amounts to nothing more than the plain Anglo-Saxon which is adopted by the resolution in respect to the statement made by Mr. Lumsden.

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: May be the hon. member will tell us what it does mean?

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: My imagination is hardly vivid enough to cope with my hon. friend's or to enable me to say what is meant by this motion.

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: It is the Prime Minister's declaration that I am asking the hon. gentleman to cope with.

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext:
My hon. friend is not obtuse. Whatever else he may be charged with, nobody has yet charged him with being obtuse and I do not intend to assume that he is guilty of any lack of

qualification that his friends have never suspected of, and even his enemies have never found him guilty of.

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: You never can be guilty of that which nature does not endow you with.

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext:
We are told that we must fear the Greeks even though they bring gifts and my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) is so lamb-like of late that I am disposed to regard him as a gentleman whom we need to watch. Now, the statement in the first part of this amendment is nothing but a reiteration in superlatives of the statement contained in the first part of the resolution of the Prime Minister, and that being so we may remove it from the controversy. But as to the second part there is a new element introduced. It says:
The cost of the eastern division of the said railway according to the latest estimates of the government will be so enormously in excess of the estimates submitted to parliament in 1904-5 as to arouse the most serious alarm.
That is a splendid phrase.

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: It is almost like the 1903 Liberal platform.

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: It won't be nearly so successful.

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext:
My hon. friends opposite are getting in training to lay down their platform next June, and I suppose that some of those glittering phrases are being prepared by the lesser members of the opposition. My hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) goes on to propose in his motion that parliament should investigate ' said charges '. What charges?
To investigate the statement made by Mr. Lumsden in his letters and all other matters connected with or related to the construction of the eastern division of the said railway and the expenditure of public moneys thereon.
Just fancy imposing on this House the task of investigating every thing connected with the railway since its inception; every dollar that has been spent on it, not in connection with its construction or the classification or the payments to contractors, but every dollar expended on the railway from 1903 to the present. - Is there any connection between that and the utterances made by Mr. Lumsden in his letters as to the engineers on sections 'B' and 'F' ? Not at all, the two things are irrelevant one to the other. Let us see what Mr. Lumsden has said. His statement is that he was dissatisfied with the failure to carry out his instructions on the part of certain gentlemen who were connected with sections 'B' and 'F'-not the whole staff, for he took good care to correct any misapprehension on that point by writing the very day after

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: he wrote that first letter that his statement did not refer to the whole staff on the system or to the whole staff on sections 'B' and 'F,' but only to a certain number of these gentlemen. Now, I find according to the estimate in the annual report of the commission for 1909, that the total mileage under construction is something like 1,800, and, giving the widest possible range to any complaint made by Mr. Lumsden it would only apply to about 500 miles. He acquits the engineering staff on the other 1,300 miles from any possible criticism; he stands by what they have done, he recommended the appointment of every one of them and he limits his criticism to the engineers working on less than one-third of the whole line. The government now propose to investigate his statements made with reference to these gentlemen. As to all other engineers Mr. Lumsden gives them a certificate of character.

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman read the certificate of character which Mr. Lumsden gives to the other engineers?

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: I have read the statement of Mr. Lumsden that his complaint only applies to certain engineers who were responsible for the measurement, classification, supervision and inspection of considerable portions in district 'B,' and east of Rennie crossing in district 'F.'

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: Is that a certificate of character for the others.

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: If Mr. Lumsden had any complaint to make about the others he would have made it, but he expressly limited his complaint to the men on these sections he has described. Now, in order to consider whether the House should adopt the second portion of the resolution of my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) for that is the only point in controversy, let us look for a moment at a few general principles. My hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) has not complained much about the government. In fact I notice that hon. gentlemen opposite who usually discuss the government with the most reckless disregard of facts are very careful to confine their complaints in this matter to the fact that the Minister of Railways did not have some one in his office to check off the statements that the commission sent over, but surely that is not a very grave thing. Under the statute the commissioners are responsible, and the Minister of Railways is simply the mouth piece in the House for the commission.

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: So he thinks.

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext:
So the statute says and the statute confirms his judgment in that regard. But, my hon. friends oppo-

site know very well that if there has been any error in regard to the question of cost the man solely responsible for that is Mr. Lumsden. My hon. friend from Hamilton is too old a railway man not to know that the Minister of Railways or the commission is no more responsiole for an engineer who in the northern wilds classifies common excavation as solid rock than would Sir Thomas Shaughnessy be for a wrong classification made by an engineer in the far west. And yet every Conservative newspaper in the country will be talking about the government and its malversation in connection with the management of the construction of this railway and of the millions of dollars of the peoples money that have been thrown away. A government or a company finds the money with which a railway is built. The contractor builds it. the engineer inspects it and determines the amount of money the contractor receives. The government or the company pays that money when the engineer certifies it. If stone develops where the estimate indicated clay, are the government or the directors of the company to be blamed? If the engineer when he comes to decide what is to be paid to the contractor for an excavation, has allowed for loose rock ot solid rock instead of common excavation, would you talk about the government or the directors of the company being turned out because the engineer has made a mistake? A company or a government is absolutely helpless if the engineers are dishonest in regard to their classification, all they can do is to dismiss the engineers. The hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) knows that the man who settles what a contractor is to receive is the engineer, not the directors of the company or the government or the commission.

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: The member for South Lanark does not know that. He always has heard, and especially from the other side of the House, of ministerial responsibility, that the party who is responsible to this House is the minister.

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: That is true. The minister is responsible for the acts of his immediate officials, upon whom he must depend, but my hon. friend has been a minister, and he wpuld have thought it very hard if he haa been constructing a railway as a government work and an engineer on the north shore of Lake Superior had classified wrongly for a contractor, if his opponents had asked that he be condemned because of that.

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: He has been in that position several times. Some of the engineers and contractors stole money and the opposition held the minister responsible.	'

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: And you disclaimed responsibility, certainly.

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: Not at all. I did not disclaim the responsibility. I made the excuse that the minister could hardly be responsible for the act. But the principle laid down is that the minister is responsible for everything done in his department and he must show the reason why.

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: Perhaps my hon. friend will tell me whether or not he was right in his contention?

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: I knew the principle was a right one.

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: But did you think you were right yourself?

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: I thought I should not be held responsible and it is the same in England. If the hon. gentleman will allow me a moment, if there is stealing in a department, say from the Navy Department, the minister who represents the government in the House is responsible. The excuse may be made that if the superintendence was as direct as the minister could possibly exercise, the party should be punished and the minister excused. Of the responsibility there is no doubt.

maintopic: THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I am at a loss to understand where my hon. friend stood as a minister, whether he assumed a certain position or whether he stood where he is now in opposition, taking any kind of position if it will hurt the government. If Mr. Lumsden had communicated to the commissioners the names of the men whom he said ought to be dismissed and had recommended their dismissal, and if the minister or commissioners, on investigation, had found the statement was correct, and did not dismiss them, then the minister or the commissioners, as the case might be, should be condemned, but as Mr. Lumsden has not indicated the names of the men in whom he has lost confidence, who the men were who disobeyed his instructions, the Prime Minister is proceeding by this inquiry to find out who these men are, and to deal with them when they are found out. My hon. friend will agree with me that even on his stand of strict ministerial responsibility the government are not and cannot be held responsible until they know the men who have done wrong, if there has been wrong.
The hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Baker) himself discussed this question of responsibility in the House two years ago, in the debate on the report of the Hodgins Committee. He discussed these letters of Mr. Woods in the following language:
The hon. member also comments upon the fact that in putting in before the committee the various letters that have been referred

to to-day. I have said that those letters did not charge or prove fraud against the commissioners; I say so still. There is nothing in those letters that indicate any fraudulent conduct on the part of the commissioners That has never been pretended.
My hon. friend did not pretend then, he cannot pretend now, that these statements in regard to excessive classification in any way, if true, would reflect on the commission or the minister, and the result is that we get down to this question as to whether or not there have been mistakes in classification, whether or not Mr. Lumsden was correct in his statement that there was disobedience of instructions and failure to record what he had told these men should be done. These are proper subjects for the committee. The question as to . whether there was proper classification is a matter entirely for the tribunal constituted by parliament in 1903. I need not read to the House again section 7 of the agreement, in which that matter was especially provided for. There is another section of the agreement, section 47, which expressly provides for another and final arbitration in the event of there being any further difference in regard to matters affecting the construction. So clear and definite was parliament in making this agreement in 1903, that they have declared in those two sections that all matters of difference in regard to construction shall be dealt with by arbitration boards.
I was surprised to hear my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) say to-day that if this matter was before the Exchequer Court, he would still have thought they should move for a committee. The statement of the member for East Hamilton in 1908 that this complaint in regard to classification did not reflect upon the commissioners and only dealt with questions as to whether the engineers did right or not, shows conclusively that it was a matter to be determined by a technical board, and if this had come before an Exchequer Court judge it is against every precedent here or in England for parliament to intervene and take out of the hands of a tribunal of the country and to itself determine a question that had been committed to a tribunal. My. hon. friend will search in vain for such a precedent. The issue is surely one for engineers to determine. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways, in his admirable speech, pointed out section 15, which provides that the chief engineer shall be the sole judge of the work as regards quantity and quality. He is the man who has to certify for every dollar of money paid to any contractor. Neither the Transcontinental commission nor the government had anything to do with certifying to these payments, "if there be anything wrong, if there be any unduly increased cost, Mr. Lumsden was the man Mr. E. M. MACDONALD.
responsible because he certified for every dollar of money paid anybody, and the other engineers had nothing to do but act under his direction. Where could you find a tribunal so well qualified to deal with the classification as that created by the agreement? The engineers who compose that tribunal are the best judges one could select. Does my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) or my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) think that any committee of this House, composed of men without any engineering training, would be able to form any better judgment on a question of classification than men specially trained to that work? Just imagine my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox), with all his judicial knowledge, taken out into the wilds of Lake Superior and asked to. decide whether or not certain material was loose rock or only common excavation. Yet that hon. gentleman would like to have himself and other members of this House, equally inexperienced, constituted a tribunal to determine whether or not the classifications arrived at were right, and actually would have us believe that a tribunal of that kind would be more competent than one composed of engineers of eminence such as Messrs. Schreiber, Grant and Kelliher. Yet that is the proposition embodied in the amendment of my hon. friend. Of course, we could subpoena the engineers who made the classification and who had seen the work done, and we could hear their testimony and weigh the balance of evidence pro and con. If there v>'as more evidence on behalf of the Transcontinental engineers than on behalf of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the evidence of these gentlemen was not shaken in any way by cross examination-my hon. friends from Simcoe and Hamilton, if they were going to be absolutely judicial, would 'be bound to find in favour of the Transcontinental engineers. But what a practical tribunal that would be, and how much light would they not throw on the question5 How convincing their judgment would be in contradistinction to that of a tribunal composed of men who have practical experience and who know all about classifying, who have had daily reports ever since the inception of the work and who have been over the road and have studied every aspect of the question* I think no one, who is not blinded by party, will fail to recognize that the latter tribunal is by far the more competent of the two. And the Minister of Railways has shown us how well the government are protected against any payments being made to the contractors which ought not to be made. Of course, our hon. friends opposite, despite their experience of two years ago, will continue to ring the changes on the cry of scandal, and will argue that the object of the government is to prevent investigation. But what

the government is doing is sending the question to the only tribunal whose verdict will be worth something as compared with that of a committee of this House. In the one case you have a body of men who can decide from practical knowledge and experience as well as from the evidence, and in the other you would simply have a committee which could only give a decision based on the evidence without having the competence or practical experience to estimate, as engineers would, the value of that evidence.
I pointed out some time ago that Mr. Lumsden had only complained with regard to two divisions. But even with regard to section ' F,' I have a letter in my hand which shows how all these imaginary charges disappear on investigation. There is a letter written 'by Mr. Woods, chief engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific, on the 21st of January:
January 21, 1910.
Gordon Grant, Esq.,
Chief Engineer, N.T.R.,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir,-Referring to my letters of July 27 and October 12 last, re classification on O'Brien, Fowler and MacDougall contract, district ' F ' to which our district engineer, Mr. Heman made objections, and particularly to my letter of October 12, wherein I specified many instances in which we objected to returns as made, I am pleased to say that since that time a further examination of the work has been made by your district and inspecting engineers, together with our district engineer, and an agreement made as to classification and other matters, satisfactory to both parties.
I am to-day in receipt of a letter from Mr. Heaman in which he states that he has written a letter to district engineer Poulin, approving the classification and other matters on the above work, as agreed by your inspecting engineer and himself, providing Mr. Balcom's assurances are carried out.
This being the case, please consider my letters referred to above, as being withdrawn.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) H. A. WOODS, Assistant Chief Engineer.
So that once these engineers, who thoroughly understand these matters, come to deal with them, they have no difficulty in reaching an adjustment; and I say that when you come to the genesis of this question, when you come to analyse the arguments of my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) and Hamilton (Mr. Barker), you find that because certain engineers on districts ' B ' and ' F ' may have made wrong classifications, the suggestion is made that they did so deliberately. That, Sir, is an unfair assumption. These men, who went into this engineering work, are not all Liberals. A great many of them are Conservatives. They belong to a profession just as honourable as that of the law and they
realize that their great asset is their honourable name and the reputation that, in dealing with questions commited to their care, they will deal with them honestly. So that every presumption we can make that is at all reasonable would go against the theory that these engineers would deliberately make wrong classifications. To lay themselves open to such an imputation would be to destroy their prospects in their profession for all time. Instead of assuming that, because there were disputes and differences between engineers representing different interests in that northern country, there was wrong-doing on the part of either or both of them, it would have been only tair and reasonable to assume that these men, or some of them, might have come to wrong conclusions, but that, whether they did or not they acted honestly in regard to the matter and believed they were doing what was right. All this shows that the whole question is one that can only be dealt with by the tribunal which parliament constituted especially to deal with it. I was surprised when the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) who had spent a great deal of time on this question, and had made an argument which might be dignified with the statement that he had made the best oE a bad case, talked about this old story of tbe government having spoken about this railway being built at a cost to the country of $13,000,000. My hon. friend had delved in the figures a great deal, but had he made this further calculation, he would have seen that the conclusion was one that nobody would believe, for it would mean that the country was to get this road at a cost of $866 per mile. To say to me or to any man that any minister of the Crown said that it was possible to build a road through that country at a cost of $866 a mile shows that the proposition was merely a ludicrous one and one that will not appeal to anybody. I do not think that anybody believed it, the hon. member himself was candid enough to say that he did not believe it. But I thought that, in referring to it, the hon. gentleman used an argument not at all necessary in what was otherwise, as I have said, about the best argument that could be made for a bad case. Nor did I take it kindly that the hon. gentleman spoke of ' stifling the Hodgins charges.' He and I sat on that committee together, and he knows that wo dealt with the question when it came before us fairly and honestly. The charges made by Mr. Hodgins were all abandoned, and the differences of opinion as to quantities were found to turn on the same question as in this case-the question whether there had been proper classification or not. And the position taken in that first case is the one to be taken now that the proper tribunal ought to deal with the sub-

ject. That was done with the Hodgins charges, and I feel sure that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lennox) believes in his heart that, had we attempted to determine that question of classification, we would have realized that we were a poor body to engage in such a duty in comparison with the tribunal appointed by the government for that purpose.
I shall not speak at greater length. I do not think hon. members opposite are very serious about this matter. They realize that the question involved is the determination of the proper amount to be paid to the contractors, and that that question is in the hands of the proper tribunal. Parliament can deal with it when that tribunal makes its report. And, if contractors have received any money that they should not have received as the result of the determination of the engineers, there are ample funds in the hands of the government to guarantee the country against loss on this account. Every interest demands the consummation of this great enterprise in the. way desired by the men on this side who have stood for it from its inception-as many men who vote Conservative stand for it to-day. There is a great revolution in public opinion on this subject since 1904. Many of those who opposed the Grand Trunk Pacific at that time are now standing for it as strongly as those who originally agitated it. The mistake hon. gentlemen opposite make is in fancying that they sire going to gather strength by appealing to the Bourbons of their party, the men who never learn and never forget. They will do better by appealing to the patriotism of all Canada, whose people look upon this as a worthy enterprise to be undertaken by this country at the beginning of the twentieth century. If they would forget their carping criticism and realize that this enterprise is going along proper lines, it would be better for themselves and better for Canada.
Mr. MIDDLEBRO moved the adjournment of the debate.
